source: Magesh, Surani, Dahl, Suzgun, Manning & Ho (2024/2025) Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools
finding: First preregistered test of commercial legal RAG tools. Retrieval lowers hallucination against a closed-book chatbot but does not remove it. Hallucination counts wrong statements AND false claims that a cited source supports a statement.
numbers: 202 queries. Hallucination: Lexis+ AI about 17%, Westlaw AI-Assisted Research about 33%, Ask Practical Law AI about 17%, GPT-4 closed-book about 43% (figure read; abstract says tools hallucinate between 17% and 33%). Accurate: Lexis 65%, Westlaw 42% (41% in one passage), Practical Law about 19-20%, GPT-4 about 49%. Practical Law gave incomplete answers on over 60%. Kappa 0.77, 85.4% agreement between graders.
quote: hallucinate between 17% and 33% of the time
limits: Small query set (202). Closed tools, so the cause of error inside retrieval vs generation is unknown. Per-tool hallucination values were read from a figure with garbled labels. GPT-4 was closed-book, not given the same corpus.
agent_relevance: Retrieving text first cuts wrong or false citations by roughly a third to a half, not to zero. The agent still needs a check that each cited case really says what is claimed (G verify).

source: Magesh et al. (2024/2025) Hallucination-Free? - misgrounding failure type
finding: The dangerous failure after retrieval is misgrounding: a real case is cited for a holding it does not contain. It is harder to spot than an invented case. Examples include citing an overruled case (Casey, overruled by Dobbs) and a rule paragraph that does not exist.
numbers: Hallucination defined as incorrect OR misgrounded. Groundedness only graded for correct responses. Errors appeared in every question category (95% CIs in Fig. 5).
limits: Qualitative examples plus category rates; not a measured before/after test of reading the case text then citing.
agent_relevance: Verification must open the cited text and compare the proposition, and must check whether the case is still good law. An existence check alone is not enough.

source: Molfetta, Cocchieri, Ragazzi, Bartolini, Patella & Moro (2026) Sycophants in the Courtroom (full text read)
finding: Tests whether LLMs defer to misleading cited authority in EU law (LEGAL-LINK-EU) versus medicine. Legal accuracy depends on supplied context: it jumps with true context and breaks with misleading context. Larger reasoning models resisted less.
numbers: LEGAL-LINK-EU: 1,127 multiple-choice items, 7 EUR-Lex relation types. Closed-book legal accuracy: Gemini-2.5-Flash 70.5%, GPT-OSS 120B 62.6%; true context adds +27.0 and +29.9 points. Medicine adds only +2.8 and +2.3 points. Parametric-override index (POI) legal: GPT-OSS 120B 43.1% vs Llama-3.1 78.2% (lower means context displaces memory more). Llama-3.1 drops to 62.1% on implicit-repeal relations.
quote: reliable context can repair legal QA but misleading citations can pull models away from correct internal beliefs
limits: Statutes and EU instruments, not case precedent. Multiple choice, zero-shot, oracle context. The CSI numbers are hard to read: the paper reports CSI 46.9% (Llama) falling to 13.4% (GPT-OSS 20B) and calls this greater over-deference. The explanation that reasoning models rationalise context is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Do not treat a retrieved or cited authority as true. A scaffold that grades the source before using it is needed, and stronger models need it more, not less.

source: Molfetta et al. (2026) Sycophants in the Courtroom - mitigation check
finding: The paper tests no mitigation. No forced steelman, devil's advocate or counter-argument prompt is evaluated. Authors list few-shot, end-to-end RAG and open-ended argument as future work.
numbers: 0 mitigation conditions. All runs zero-shot with oracle contexts.
quote: Second, we strictly employ zero-shot prompting and oracle contexts
limits: Absence of evidence in this paper only. It does not show that a steelman fails.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open: a steelman step in the agent would be an untested design, to be measured with an agent test.

source: Hassid, Synnaeve, Adi & Schwartz (2025/2026) Dont Overthink It: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: Within one question, shorter sampled reasoning chains are more often correct than longer ones. Taking the shortest of several samples beats random and longest picks.
numbers: Four reasoning LLMs, four benchmarks (math plus GPQA-D). Shortest chain beats random by up to 18.8 points and longest by up to 34.5 points. Shortest chains are 50% and 67% shorter than random and longest. Average gain of shortest over random 2.2 to 15.7 points on math.
quote: taking the shortest answer for each question strongly and consistently outperforms
limits: Math and science QA, not legal analogy. Longer reasoning is still needed for harder questions across questions, so length predicts error within a question, not across questions or models. Observational.
agent_relevance: Supports a stop or re-check trigger based on length relative to the agent's own other samples, not an absolute token cap. Fits the gpt-5 result (wrong answers 45% longer).

source: Hassid et al. (2025/2026) short-m@k method and fine-tuning check
finding: A usable control rule: run k samples in parallel, stop when the first m finish, vote among those m. Fine-tuning on shortest chains also helps.
numbers: Six reasoning LLMs. short-1@k matches majority voting with up to 40% less compute (LN-Super-49B). short-3@k beats majority voting at all compute budgets and runs up to 33% faster. Qwen-2.5 7B and 32B fine-tuned on S1-short got shorter thinking and better scores; S1-long gave no significant gain.
limits: Needs parallel sampling. Tested on math and GPQA, not legal tasks. Backtracking analysis: shorter chains have fewer backtracks.
agent_relevance: Cheap trigger for a re-check: if the first answer took much more thinking than sibling samples, distrust it.

source: Zhang & Ashley (2026) Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs? - limitations section
finding: Authors state that factor readout was tested only on controlled, generated English trade-secret narratives. No intervention (suppress or amplify a feature) was run. Intervention tests are listed as future work.
numbers: 26 factors; three open models 1.7B to 8B; train and test passages share one generation procedure; TF-IDF also strong; some positive and negative passages differ in length.
quote: Intervention experiments that suppress or amplify a selected feature would test whether a model's outputs depend on it.
limits: Own limitations statement. Real judicial opinions and larger models untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: factor structure is decodable (correlation) but not shown to be used. Gap 1 partly answered: no real-opinion extraction result from this group yet.

source: Wang et al. (2026) LePREC: Reasoning as Classification over Structured Factors (abstract page)
finding: A group apparently outside Pittsburgh uses LLM-extracted question-answer factors plus a sparse linear model to pick relevant legal issues in real court cases. Claims large gains over GPT-4o and Claude.
numbers: 769 real Malaysian Contract Act cases, expert-annotated. GPT-4o precision 62%. Reported 30-40% improvement over advanced LLM baselines (exact LePREC figure not on the abstract page).
limits: Abstract page only. Task is issue identification, not HYPO/CATO distinguishing. Not a replication of Zhang et al. Affiliation not checked.
agent_relevance: Factor extraction by LLM then a transparent scorer works on real opinions in another jurisdiction: partial support for extract factors, then compare, as a scaffold.

source: Cao et al. (2026) ACAL: Adaptive Collaboration of Argumentative LLMs (abstract page)
finding: Multi-agent pro and con argument teams settled in a quantitative bipolar argumentation graph, with escalation of borderline cases. Evaluated on LegalBench only; baselines CoT and RAG. No factor or precedent test.
numbers: No numbers on the page; claims to beat strong baselines on Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite and Gemini-2.5-Flash.
agent_relevance: A structured both-sides debate is being tried, but with no measure of sycophancy to authority. Not evidence for a steelman effect.

source: Yu, Quartey & Schilder (2022) Legal Prompting: Teaching a Language Model to Think Like a Lawyer
finding: Prompts that name legal reasoning steps (issue, rule, application, conclusion variants) lift GPT-3 zero-shot on a statute entailment task. Plain zero-shot chain-of-thought is weaker and inconsistent.
numbers: COLIEE entailment, GPT-3. Zero-shot CoT accuracy 0.6296 (2021 test) and 0.7064 (2022 test). Best legal prompt (TRRAC) beats the 2021 COLIEE winner by 15.79%. IRREAC/IRRAC beat the 2022 winner by 5.41%; 8-shot best for 2022 at +9.46%. Zero-shot CoT beat the 2022 winner by 4.05% but lost to the 2021 winner by 17.65%. Fine-tuning with GPT-3's own explanations was worse than labels alone.
limits: Old model (GPT-3), statute entailment, not precedent analogy. Gains over competition winners compare different test years and systems.
agent_relevance: Naming the reasoning move in the prompt helps on a legal task. Nobody here tested analogise or distinguish moves on case pairs.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Asking the model to recall similar problems before solving them beats plain zero-shot CoT. Self-generated exemplars beat retrieved ones for strong models and lose for weak ones.
numbers: GSM8K accuracy: text-davinci-003 0-shot 14%, 0-shot CoT 50%, 5-shot fixed 54%, 5-shot retrieved 57%, self-generated 61%. text-davinci-002: 13, 22, 43, 47, 48. text-curie-001: 2, 2, 2, 3, 2. Also MATH, Codeforces, BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, PaLM 2-L.
limits: Math and code. Analogy means recalled solved problems, not legal distinguishing. Retrieval used top-5 Sentence-BERT neighbours.
agent_relevance: Supports a map-an-analogue step for strong models. For weaker models, retrieve real cases instead of letting the model invent them.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) number of self-generated exemplars K
finding: One exemplar is worse than several. Best results at K = 3 to 5.
numbers: Table 5 first columns: GSM8K K=1 76.1, K=2 77.0; MATH K=1 34.8, K=2 36.7; text says K at least 3 is stable and K=3 or 5 best.
limits: Self-generated exemplars, not retrieved cases. The model for Table 5 and the K=3 to 5 values were not confirmed in the text read.
agent_relevance: A default of about 3 analogues, not 1 and not 32, is reasonable. Memento (K=0 59.9, K=4 64.5, K=32 63.9) agrees that gains flatten after a few.

source: Zhao et al. (2023) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners - raw cases versus insights
finding: Abstracted insights and recalled trajectories each help, with different strengths by task. Insights matter more where general guidance applies, recalled cases matter more where precise action sequences matter.
numbers: Insights-only / retrieval-only success: HotpotQA 36% / 31%; ALFWorld 50% / 55%; WebShop 37% / 38% (score 0.675 / 0.67). Both together best on all three. gpt-3.5-turbo agents.
limits: Agent tasks, not law. Standard errors and sample sizes in figures not read. The same group designed both modes.
agent_relevance: Keep both a rule memory and a raw-case memory; do not expect one to dominate. Pick by task type.

finding: Retrieval relevance matters: task-similar cases beat random cases by a wide margin. Model-written insights beat hand-written ones. Adding reflections to insight writing hurt.
numbers: HotpotQA SR%: ReAct 28.0, hand-crafted insights 32.0, insights with reflections 29.0, gpt-3.5 insights 32.0, ExpeL 39.0. ALFWorld SR%: ReAct 40.0, reasoning-similarity retrieval 48.5, random cases 42.5, task-similarity retrieval (ExpeL) 59.0. Insights extracted from only the few-shot examples gave no advantage over ReAct.
limits: Small agent benchmarks, gpt-3.5. Number of retrieved examples k was a parameter, not ablated in the text read.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant analogues add little (42.5 vs 40.0); relevance of the retrieved case is the lever. Distilled rules need real experience to distil from.

source: Pipitone & Alami (2024) LegalBench-RAG: A Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Legal Domain
finding: Retrieval of exact legal text spans is hard. Recall rises and precision falls as k grows from 1 to 64. A general reranker made results worse than none.
numbers: 6,889 question-answer pairs, 714 documents, 4 datasets. PrivacyQA easiest: Precision@1 14.38%, Recall@64 84.19%. MAUD hardest: Precision@1 2.65%, Recall@64 28.28%. Best setup: recursive character splitter, no reranker.
limits: Contracts and policy text, not case law. Measures retrieval, not answer quality, so best k for reasoning is not given.
agent_relevance: Choice of K is a precision-recall trade; the right K for reasoning must be measured on the downstream answer, not retrieval scores.

source: Nay et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Tax Attorneys (abstract and method text)
finding: Each newer OpenAI model did better on tax-law questions. Giving the relevant legal text and few-shot examples raised GPT-4. Still below expert tax lawyers.
numbers: Automated grading by a GPT-4 judge, error under 1% on a validation subset. Accuracy tables not extracted.
limits: Statute application, not precedent. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Retrieved authority text plus examples is the lever for statute tasks; weak evidence for case analogy.
